extracts.text: Language moves down time in a current of its own making. It has a drift. If there were no breaking up of a language into dialects, if each language continued as a firm, self-contained unity, it would still be constantly moving away from any assignable norm, developing new features unceasingly and gradually transforming itself into a language so different from its starting point as to be in effect a new language.
extracts.who: Edward Sapir, Language: An Introduction to the Study of Speech (Project Gutenberg edition)

questions.onCorrect: Sapir treats change as something a language does by itself, and dialects arise when groups drift apart. Change does not depend on contact or on carelessness.

misconceptions.feedback: Sapir says the opposite. Without any breaking up, he says, a language would still be moving away from any fixed norm.

It would keep changing until it became in effect a new language

hints: Look at how tres and three begin.

questions.prompt: Latin p in pater matches which English sound at the start of father?
hints: Compare the first sound of pater and father.
questions.onCorrect: The p / f match recurs in pes and foot and in piscis and fish.

questions.prompt: Latin caput, cornu and pes each have two English relatives in this list of six words. Which came down from the common ancestor, and which were borrowed from Latin after the sound change?
hints: Inherited words show the changed sound at the start, and borrowed ones keep the Latin sound.

questions.onCorrect: A regular sound change touches every inherited word, so a word that keeps the Latin sound stands out as a loan. That is how the exceptions teach us how a word arrived.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Head, horn and foot are inherited, with h, h and f where Latin has k, k and p. Capital, unicorn and pedestrian are borrowed, and they keep the Latin c, c and p.

items.label: head
items.explanation: It has h where Latin caput has k, the regular match for an inherited word.

items.label: capital
items.explanation: It keeps the c of Latin caput, a sign that it arrived after the change.

items.label: horn
items.explanation: It has h where Latin cornu has k, so it went through the change.

items.label: unicorn
items.explanation: It keeps the c of Latin cornu, so it came in after the change.

items.label: foot
items.explanation: It has f where Latin pes has p, the regular match.

items.label: pedestrian
items.explanation: It keeps the p of Latin pes, so it is a loan.

questions.onCorrect: Adults say “went”, so the child must have produced “goed” from a rule, and that is what makes the error informative.

misconceptions.feedback: Adults say “went”, so a child who says “goed” can't have picked the word up from them.
“Goed” is go with the past ending added, the way walk becomes walked, so no second verb is involved.

acceptedIdeas: The child added the regular past ending -ed to go
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child added the regular past ending -ed to go

choices.label: The child heard adults say it and copied them
The child added the regular past ending -ed to go
The child mixed up go with another irregular verb

questions.prompt: A wug test might use a creature called a “bik”, /bɪk/. What is the plural ending sound an English speaker would use?
hints: Is the last sound of “bik” voiced or voiceless?
questions.onCorrect: The final /k/ is voiceless, so the plural ending is voiceless, and a child who says “biks” with /s/ has used the rule on a new word.

The extra vowel is only needed after a hissing sound.

questions.prompt: A child’s past tense of go passes through stages. In what order do these happen?
hints: At the first stage the child has no rule at all.
A form such as “goed” can only exist once the rule does.
questions.onCorrect: The dip in the middle is a sign of progress, since “goed” can only come from a rule the child has worked out. At the first stage “went” is a form repeated without any rule behind it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child first repeats “went”, then works out the -ed rule, then applies it to go and says “goed”, and last keeps the rule while saying “went” again.

items: The child repeats “went” as adults say it
The child works out the -ed rule from verbs such as “walked”

hints: Does any adult say “sheeps”?
questions.onCorrect: The child has the rule that a plural adds -s and applies it to an exception, so the error shows what the child has learned.

misconceptions.feedback: No adult says “sheeps”, so there is nothing for the child to have copied.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child applied a rule

questions.prompt: What is the plural ending sound of “gutch”?
hints: The last sound of “gutch” is /tʃ/, a hushing sound.
questions.onCorrect: After a sibilant the plural needs an extra vowel, so the child who answers “gutches” has applied the full rule.

misconceptions.feedback: A bare /z/ would run into the /tʃ/. The ending needs an extra vowel after a hissing sound.
A plain /s/ would run into the /tʃ/ at the end. After a hissing sound the ending needs a vowel.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: /ɪz/

questions.prompt: A pictured creature is “zibbing”, from a verb /zɪb/, and a child is asked what it did yesterday: “It ___.” Which ending sound goes on /zɪb/ to make the past tense?
hints: The sound before the ending is /b/. Apply the same idea as for the plural.
questions.onCorrect: The past-tense ending takes the voicing of the sound before it, as the plural does, so it is voiced after the voiced /b/.

misconceptions.feedback: /t/ would follow a voiceless sound, but /b/ is voiced.
The extra vowel appears only when the verb already ends in a t or a d sound, and /zɪb/ ends in neither.

questions.prompt: Jespersen reports a child who says “I sticked it in” and at once corrects it. What does that suggest about the child?
hints: Ask where “sticked” could have come from if adults say “stuck”.
A child who corrects a form must know something about the form that replaces it.

extracts.text: Frequently children, after giving a form which their own ears tell them is wrong, at once correct it: ‘I sticked it in--I stuck it in.’
extracts.who: Otto Jespersen, Language: Its Nature, Development and Origin (Project Gutenberg edition)
extracts.kind: A book on the nature and history of language

questions.onCorrect: The child has the adult form stuck and also a rule that adds -ed, and the rule produced sticked before the ear caught it. Children’s mistakes follow patterns, which is why they are evidence of what the child knows.

misconceptions.feedback: The child corrected the first form, so the child could tell them apart. Jespersen says the child’s own ears told him it was wrong.
Making a form from a rule and then checking it against the adult form shows two kinds of knowledge at work, which is a sign of progress.
Adults say “stuck”, and nothing in the passage mentions a book. The form “sticked” came from the child’s own rule.

acceptedIdeas: The child knows the adult form and also has a rule that made “sticked”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child knows the adult form and also has a rule that made “sticked”

choices.label: The child cannot tell the two forms apart
The child’s speech is getting worse
The child learned “sticked” from an adult and “stuck” from a book
The child knows the adult form and also has a rule that made “sticked”

questions.prompt: A child says “mouses”. What does this show about the child?
hints: The child has made a plural, but not the adult one.
questions.onCorrect: The child has the -s plural rule and applies it to a noun that is an exception.

misconceptions.feedback: The child has formed a plural by adding the regular ending, which shows the opposite.
Adults say “mice”, so there is no adult form to copy.
Overregularisation is typical of normal development.

acceptedIdeas: The child has learned the regular plural rule
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child has learned the regular plural rule

choices.label: The child has a speech problem that needs help
The child is copying the way adults talk
The child has learned the regular plural rule
The child cannot yet form plurals at all

questions.prompt: A child is shown a cartoon creature, told its name, and asked to complete “There are two ___”. What is this test called, after the made-up name?
hints: It is named for the creature in the first picture.
questions.onCorrect: Berko's test shows that children apply a rule to a word they have not heard, which imitation alone cannot explain.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are other creatures in the same study. The test took its popular name from the first creature in this lesson.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The wug test.

questions.prompt: Think of a speaker who says “floor” with the r sounded in one setting. What about the same speaker in another setting?
hints: Think of how your own speech changes between a job interview and a chat with friends.
questions.onCorrect: Speakers move between pronunciations depending on the setting, which is why a feature can be a variable and not a fixed property of a person.

misconceptions.feedback: Speakers shift their pronunciation with the setting, speaking more carefully in some situations than in others, so one person can sound the r at one moment and drop it at another.
A speaker who sounds the r in one setting may well sound it in others too; what changes from setting to setting is how often.

acceptedIdeas: They might leave the r out, depending on the setting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They might leave the r out, depending on the setting

choices.label: They will always sound the r, since a pronunciation is fixed for each person
They might leave the r out, depending on the setting
They will always leave the r out in any other setting

questions.prompt: A speaker from Glasgow and a speaker from London both say “I've lost my keys”, with the same words and grammar, but their vowels and their r sound different. What kind of difference is this?
hints: Which of the three names a difference in pronunciation only?
questions.onCorrect: An accent is a way of pronouncing the language, and a dialect adds its own words and grammar to the pronunciation.

misconceptions.feedback: A dialect differs in vocabulary and grammar as well. Here the words and grammar are the same.
Register depends on the situation, such as a formal or casual one, and not on which speaker it is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accent

questions.prompt: One speaker says “sidewalk” and “I've gotten better” where another says “pavement” and “I've got better”. What kind of variation separates their speech?
hints: It involves words and grammar as well as sound.
questions.onCorrect: A dialect has its own vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation, and a speaker of one is not making mistakes in another.

misconceptions.feedback: An accent is a difference in pronunciation only. A different word and a different grammar are more than that.
A register is the variety one speaker chooses for a situation. Nothing here says the situation differs.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dialect

hints: Read the three bars in order of the stores' status.

questions.prompt: A visitor says that the speech of a poor, unschooled community must be cruder than the speech of a city. What would Sapir say about that?
hints: Find what Sapir says about complex types of language and the level of cultural advance.
The pairing of Plato with a swineherd says that the two are alike in one respect.

extracts.text: Both simple and complex types of language of an indefinite number of varieties may be found spoken at any desired level of cultural advance. When it comes to linguistic form, Plato walks with the Macedonian swineherd, Confucius with the head-hunting savage of Assam.
extracts.who: Edward Sapir, Language: An Introduction to the Study of Speech (Project Gutenberg edition)

questions.onCorrect: Sapir finds complex forms among speakers at every level of culture, so the form of a variety gives no ground for ranking its speakers. The same reasoning applies to the claim that a standard variety is better in itself.

misconceptions.feedback: Sapir says the opposite. Simple and complex types of language are found at any level of cultural advance.
Nothing in the passage ties complexity to writing. Sapir’s point is that linguistic form does not follow the level of culture.
Standard varieties are not mentioned. Sapir says complex forms occur at every level of culture, whether or not a variety is the standard.

acceptedIdeas: Form gives no ground for the ranking, since complex language is found at every level of culture
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Form gives no ground for the ranking, since complex language is found at every level of culture

choices.label: The visitor is right, since a language grows more complex as its speakers become more learned
The visitor should judge by the community’s writing, since writing marks a complex language
Only a standard variety can be called complex, so the visitor is half right

questions.prompt: A doctor uses technical terms when talking to colleagues and plain everyday words when talking to a patient's family. What is this variation by situation called?
hints: The speaker is the same. What changes is the setting.
questions.onCorrect: Register is the variety a speaker chooses to suit a situation, and every speaker has more than one.

misconceptions.feedback: A dialect belongs to a community of speakers. This is one speaker adjusting to a situation.
The difference here is in words and style as well as pronunciation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Register.

questions.prompt: Six cases of variation are listed. Which are differences of accent, which of dialect and which of register?
hints: Ask whether the difference is in sound only, in words or grammar as well, or in the situation.
A register changes within one speaker, while an accent and a dialect belong to a community.
questions.onCorrect: An accent differs in sound only, a dialect also in words and grammar, and a register in the speaker’s choice for a situation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Glasgow and London vowels and the two pronunciations of “bath” are accents. “Lorry” and “I seen it” are dialect. The lawyer and the student are shifting register.

items.explanation: One speaker changes variety to suit the situation.

items.label: A speaker says “I seen it” where another says “I saw it”
items.explanation: A difference of grammar is more than a difference of sound.

items.label: A student speaks carefully in a job interview and casually with friends
items.explanation: The same speaker moves between varieties as the situation changes.

items.label: Two speakers say “bath” with different vowel sounds and no other difference

questions.prompt: Which sound did Labov count in “fourth floor”?
hints: It occurs after a vowel, in two places in the phrase.
questions.onCorrect: Labov counted whether the r after a vowel was pronounced, in the middle of “fourth” and at the end of “floor”.

misconceptions.feedback: The l is in floor, but Labov was counting a sound that occurs in both words, after the vowel.
The th is in the phrase, but Labov was counting a sound that comes after a vowel, in two places in the phrase.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The r after a vowel

questions.prompt: In Labov’s study the second, more careful answer had more r’s than the first. What does that suggest?
hints: Ask what was different between the first answer and the second.
A shift in the same person between two settings shows that the feature is a variable.
questions.onCorrect: Speakers of every group shifted towards the prestige variant when they spoke carefully, which is what makes the r a social signal and not a fixed trait of a person.

misconceptions.feedback: Labov asked an ordinary question and did not say what he was counting. The pattern showed up without anyone being told what to look for.
The same person pronounced the r more often in the careful answer than in the first, so the pronunciation shifted with the setting.
The r-less pronunciation is not a mistake. In another place or time it can carry the prestige, and speakers shift towards whichever variant is prestigious where they live.

acceptedIdeas: Speakers moved towards the prestige pronunciation when careful
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Speakers moved towards the prestige pronunciation when careful

Each employee has one fixed pronunciation of the r
Speakers moved towards the prestige pronunciation when careful

questions.prompt: Compare nimesoma, “I have read”, with nitasoma, “I will read”. Where in the word does the difference lie?
hints: Write the two words one above the other and mark the letters that differ.
questions.onCorrect: Only the middle changes, me to ta, so that part must carry the difference between have read and will read.

misconceptions.feedback: Both words begin with ni, which fits the I they share in translation.
Both words end in soma, which fits the read they share in translation.
Most of the two words is identical, with the same start and the same ending, and only two letters differ.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the middle

questions.prompt: Compare walisoma, “they read”, and tulipika, “we cooked”, with the forms that have -me- and -ta-. What does the middle part -li- mark?
hints: Look at the tense of the two translations that have -li-.
questions.onCorrect: Both forms with -li- translate as a simple past, read and cooked, while -me- goes with have read and -ta- with will read, so -li- marks the past.

misconceptions.feedback: The perfect is the marker -me-, which goes with have read. The forms with -li- translate as read and cooked, with no have.
The future is -ta-, as in nitasoma, “I will read”. Neither form with -li- has will in its translation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Past

questions.prompt: What does tu- mean?
hints: Remove the parts you already know and see what is left.
questions.onCorrect: Once the past marker and the verb are accounted for, the prefix tu- is left to carry the meaning we.

misconceptions.feedback: They is wa-, which you can see in walisoma. The prefix here is tu-.
I is ni-, in nimesoma and nitasoma.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We.

questions.prompt: How do you say “they cooked”?
hints: Take the subject for they, the marker for the past and the stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The form is built from wa- for they, -li- for the past and -pika for cook, so the new word needs no new part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “we cooked”. The subject for they is wa-.
That is “they read”. The stem for cook is -pika.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: walipika.

questions.prompt: Use the pieces: how do you say “s/he has cooked”?
hints: Subject for s/he, marker for the perfect, stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The form is a- for s/he, -me- for the perfect and -pika for cook, assembled in that order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “s/he has read”. The stem for cook is -pika.
The prefix tu- means we. The subject for s/he is a-.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: amepika.

questions.prompt: How do you say “they have read” in Swahili, as a verb whose subject is watoto, “children”?
hints: Subject for they, marker for perfect, stem for read.
questions.onCorrect: The verb takes wa- when its subject is a plural of people, so watoto wamesoma means the children have read.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “they read”, with the past marker. The question asks for the perfect, -me-.
The prefix tu- means we, not they.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: wamesoma.

questions.prompt: Using the data, how do you say “we have cooked” in Swahili?
hints: Take the subject for we, the marker for the perfect and the stem for cook.
questions.onCorrect: The subject tu- appears in tulipika, the perfect marker -me- in nimesoma, and -pika in the same word as tu-, so every part is given.

misconceptions.feedback: That is “we cooked”, with the past marker -li-. The question asks for the perfect, -me-.
The prefix ni- means I. The subject for we is tu-.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: tumepika.

questions.prompt: A learner sees that walisoma means “they read” and guesses that -li- marks “they”. Which form in the data is evidence against her guess?
hints: A counterexample must contain -li- and still not mean “they”.
Look at the forms with -li- and check their translations.
questions.onCorrect: Tulipika contains -li- and means “we cooked”, so -li- cannot mean “they”. What walisoma and tulipika share is the past tense, while wa- and tu- carry the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: It has no -li- in it, so it can neither support nor contradict a guess about -li-.
It holds -me- and no -li-, so it says nothing about the guess. A counterexample must contain -li-.
It holds -ta- and no -li-, so it cannot test the guess either.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: tulipika, “we cooked”

questions.prompt: Eight pieces of the Swahili verbs in the data are listed. Which are subject prefixes, which tense markers and which verb stems?
hints: Every verb has the same order: a subject prefix, then a tense marker, then a stem.
The piece that stays the same across different subjects and tenses is the stem.
questions.onCorrect: Every verb in the data has the same order, with the subject first, the tense in the middle and the stem last. That regularity is what lets you build a form such as tumepika.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pieces ni-, tu- and wa- are subject prefixes. The pieces -me-, -li- and -ta- are tense markers. The pieces -soma and -pika are verb stems.

items.label: tu- (we), as in tulipika
items.explanation: It comes first in the verb and means we.

items.label: wa- (they), as in walisoma
items.explanation: It comes first and marks the subject they.

items.label: -me- (perfect), as in umesoma
items.explanation: It sits in the middle and changes with the tense.

items.label: -li- (past), as in walisoma
items.explanation: The same piece appears with different subjects and always marks the past.

items.label: -ta- (future), as in nitasoma
items.explanation: It sits in the middle and marks the future.

items.label: -soma (read), as in amesoma
items.explanation: It stays constant across subjects and tenses, and it means read.

items.label: -pika (cook), as in tulipika
items.explanation: It is the constant part of the verbs for cook.

questions.prompt: What is the manner of articulation of /v/, as in “van”?
hints: The screen on voicing paired /v/ with another sound that differs from it in voicing alone.

questions.onCorrect: /v/ is the voiced partner of /f/, so the air hisses through a narrow channel between the lip and the teeth, and that is what makes it a fricative.

misconceptions.feedback: For a stop the airway is closed completely for a moment. You can hold /v/ for as long as you have breath, so the air is never blocked.
A nasal lets the air out through the nose with the mouth closed. For /v/ the air leaves through the mouth.

hints: Ask what stays the same and what changes between the two readings.

The words can be spoken in two orders

questions.prompt: Which of these situations makes “Sam sold a car” true and “Sam sold the old car to Lee” false?
hints: Keep the first sentence true, then change something the second sentence mentions.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sam sold a new car to Ana

If Sam sold no car, the first sentence is false here too. The situation has to keep the first sentence true.

He says “two luns”, ending in /z/, for a creature called a lun

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voicing separates /s/ from /z/ and /p/ from /b/.

flashcards.front: Name the place of articulation of /p/, /b/ and /m/.
flashcards.back: They are made by closing both lips, so they are bilabial.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are made by closing both lips, so they are bilabial.

flashcards.front: How many sounds are in “ship”, /ʃɪp/?
flashcards.back: The word has four letters and three sounds, because sh is one sound.

flashcards.front: What do we call two words that differ in exactly one sound and have different meanings?
flashcards.back: A minimal pair shows that the two sounds that differ are separate phonemes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A minimal pair shows that the two sounds that differ are separate phonemes.

flashcards.front: What is the plural ending sound after a voiced sound such as the /ɡ/ of “dog”?
flashcards.back: The ending takes on the voicing of the sound before it, which gives /z/.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ending takes on the voicing of the sound before it, which gives /z/.

flashcards.front: Why are aspirated and unaspirated /p/ called allophones and not separate phonemes in English?
flashcards.back: Speakers hear both as /p/ because the choice between them is set by position and never separates two English words.

flashcards.front: What is the smallest unit of form that carries meaning or grammatical function?
flashcards.back: A word may have one morpheme or several, and morphemes are counted by meaning and not by syllables.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A word may have one morpheme or several, and morphemes are counted by meaning and not by syllables.

flashcards.front: What is an affix that makes a new word, often in a new category, called: inflectional or derivational?
flashcards.back: Happy becomes happiness, so -ness is derivational, while -ed on walk gives the same verb in the past tense.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Happy becomes happiness, so -ness is derivational, while -ed on walk gives the same verb in the past tense.

flashcards.front: Why does “unbreakable” have four syllables and three morphemes?
flashcards.back: Syllables are beats of sound and morphemes are meaningful parts, and the two don't have to line up.

flashcards.front: What is a group of words that works as a single unit in a sentence called?
flashcards.back: A group is a constituent when a single word can replace it or the whole group can be moved together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A group is a constituent when a single word can replace it or the whole group can be moved together.

flashcards.front: What is a sentence with one string of words and two structures called: structurally what?
flashcards.back: It is structurally ambiguous: the same words can group in two ways, which gives two meanings.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same words can group in two ways, which gives two meanings.

flashcards.front: How does the substitution test show that “the small dog” is a unit but “small dog chased” is not?
flashcards.back: A single word like “it” can replace the first, and no single word can replace the second, because it cuts across two groups.

flashcards.front: What is the usual order of subject, object and verb in a plain declarative sentence called?
flashcards.back: It is the language's basic word order, which is SVO in English and SOV in Japanese.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the language's basic word order, which is SVO in English and SOV in Japanese.

flashcards.front: What is a rule called that can apply to its own output?
flashcards.back: Recursion lets a phrase contain a phrase of the same kind, so a sentence has no longest form.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A recursive rule lets a phrase contain a phrase of the same kind, so a sentence has no longest form.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't recursion mean every sentence has to be long?
flashcards.back: Recursion is a feature of the rule, and a speaker uses it as much as they need, so most sentences are short.

flashcards.front: If sentence A is true then B must be true. What relation does A have to B?
flashcards.back: The relation is entailment: A entails B when no situation makes A true and B false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A entails B when no situation makes A true and B false.

flashcards.front: What is the thing in the world that a phrase picks out called: sense or reference?
flashcards.back: The morning star and the evening star have the same reference, Venus, and different senses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The morning star and the evening star have the same reference, Venus, and different senses.

flashcards.front: Why does “It is a poodle” entail “It is a dog” but not the other way?
flashcards.back: Every situation where it is a poodle is a situation where it is a dog, but a dog can be some other breed.

flashcards.front: What is something a speaker conveys beyond what the sentence entails, which can be cancelled, called?
flashcards.back: An implicature depends on the hearer assuming the speaker is cooperative.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An implicature depends on the hearer assuming the speaker is cooperative.

flashcards.front: Which of Grice's maxims asks the speaker to be relevant?
flashcards.back: The four maxims are Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The four maxims are Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner.

flashcards.front: How does the cancel test separate an entailment from an implicature?
flashcards.back: Add a phrase that denies the consequence: a contradiction means it was entailed, and no contradiction means it was only implicated.

flashcards.front: What do we call a word in two languages that descends from one word in their common ancestor?
flashcards.back: A cognate, such as Latin pater beside English father, is related by descent and not by borrowing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cognates such as Latin pater and English father are related by descent and not by borrowing.

flashcards.front: Latin p corresponds to which English sound, as in pater and father?
flashcards.back: Latin p corresponds to English f, and the match is regular, which is why it can be used to predict forms.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match is regular, which is why it can be used to predict forms.

flashcards.front: Why can't the similarity of pater and father be a coincidence?
flashcards.back: The same match appears in many pairs, such as pes and foot and piscis and fish, and only a shared ancestor and regular change explain it.

flashcards.front: What do we call applying a rule to a word that is an exception, as in “goed”?
flashcards.back: This is overregularisation, and the error is evidence that the child has learned the rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The error is evidence that the child has learned the rule.

flashcards.front: What test asks a child to complete “two ___” for a made-up creature?
flashcards.back: In the wug test, a child who says “wugs” has not heard the word before, so must be applying a rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A child who says “wugs” has not heard the word before, so must be applying a rule.

flashcards.front: Explain, in your own words, why “goed” is evidence of rule learning.
flashcards.back: No adult says “goed”, so a child who says it has made the form with a rule that the child worked out for itself.

flashcards.front: What do we call a way of pronouncing a language, with the same words and grammar?
flashcards.back: An accent differs in sound only, while a dialect also has its own vocabulary and grammar.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An accent differs in sound only, while a dialect also has its own vocabulary and grammar.

flashcards.front: In Labov's study, which store had the highest share of employees pronouncing the r?
flashcards.back: The share was highest at Saks, the highest-ranked store, and lowest in the lowest-ranked one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The share was highest in the highest-ranked store and lowest in the lowest-ranked one.

flashcards.front: Why isn't a standard variety better in itself than a non-standard one?
flashcards.back: It is favoured because of the status of the people who use it, and linguistically every variety works equally well for its speakers.

flashcards.front: What is a table of the forms of a word, or of a set of words, called?
flashcards.back: A paradigm sets forms side by side so you can see which part changes with what.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A paradigm sets forms side by side so you can see which part changes with what.

flashcards.front: In Swahili, which prefix means “they” in walisoma?
flashcards.back: The prefix wa is the subject for they and also the plural of nouns like mtoto.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The prefix wa- is the subject for they and also the plural of nouns like mtoto.

flashcards.front: Why is it better to compare the parts of the forms than to read the translations alone?
flashcards.back: The translations say what a form means, but only lining up the forms shows which part carries which meaning, so a new form can be built.
